title: Friends with few trade benefits
gist: US free trade agreements no longer shield partners from executive tariffs (IEEPA, Sections 232/122/301/338) layered on top of FTA preferences; product mix now matters more than FTA status, and even USMCA protection is eroding after Section 338 tariffs on Canadian goods and US non-renewal in July.

insights.claim: Since January 2025 the Trump administration has imposed tariffs on nearly all partners using IEEPA, Section 232, Section 122, Section 301 and Section 338, shifting trade policy to executive authority rather than FTAs or Congress.
insights.speaker: mchalecki
insights.so_what: Tariff risk is policy-by-executive and can change at any time — price in persistent headline volatility for importers.

insights.claim: FTAs remove the MFN tariff but not executive-imposed tariffs: a Bahraini copper faucet avoids the 4% MFN rate yet pays the 50% Section 232 tariff; a Colombian napkin avoids 3.3% MFN but pays 12.5% Section 301.
insights.speaker: mchalecki
insights.so_what: FTA preference is worth only a few points against large executive tariffs — don't over-value FTA status in supply-chain decisions.
insights.quote: In short, the free trade discount remains—but so does the additional tariff.
insights.locator: In short, the free trade discount remains

insights.claim: The US still has fourteen comprehensive FTAs with twenty economies, but they no longer provide the certainty partners expect.
insights.speaker: mchalecki
insights.so_what: Reduced value of US FTAs weakens a pillar of nearshoring/friend-shoring investment cases.
insights.locator: Though the United States still has fourteen

insights.claim: From January 2025 to January 2026 the average US import tariff rose from 2.2% to 9.9%, while the average for the twenty FTA partners rose from 0.2% to 4.6% — a more than 2,000% increase versus 345% overall.
insights.speaker: mchalecki
insights.so_what: FTA partners saw the sharpest proportional shock; margin pressure concentrated in firms that assumed FTA protection.

insights.claim: Modeling a full year of 2026 tariffs, some FTA partner countries face additional tariff rates near 35%, because export composition matters more than FTA status.
insights.speaker: mchalecki
insights.so_what: Screen exposure by product (metals, autos) not by country agreement.
insights.quote: Because what a country exports matters more than whether it has a free trade agreement.
insights.locator: And the additional tariffs can, in fact

insights.claim: Bahrain shipped $365 million of unwrought aluminum to the US in 2025 and paid the 50% Section 232 tariff despite its FTA; South Korea's $30 billion of passenger vehicles avoided 2.5% MFN but paid 15% Section 232.
insights.speaker: mchalecki
insights.so_what: Aluminum and autos remain the heaviest-tariffed FTA flows — watch Korean automakers' US margins.

insights.claim: Colombia, Panama and Chile faced only about 3.5% average tariffs from April 2025 to April 2026, mainly because their exports (crude oil, coffee, precious metals) are largely exempt from Section 301/232 tariffs, not because of their FTAs.
insights.speaker: mchalecki
insights.so_what: Commodity exporters with exempt goods are relative winners; exemptions are the key variable to track.

insights.claim: USMCA, covering nearly $1 trillion in trade, has kept the average tariff on Canadian and Mexican imports at 3.8% versus roughly 30% without it, as USMCA-claimed goods are exempt from IEEPA, Section 122 and Section 301 tariffs.
insights.speaker: mchalecki
insights.so_what: USMCA compliance is worth ~26 points of tariff — rules-of-origin qualification is a material earnings driver for North American manufacturers.
insights.locator: There is, however, one major exception

insights.claim: On July 20 Trump announced 50% Section 338 tariffs on about $20 billion of Canadian imports, including for the first time goods imported under USMCA; the US also declined to renew USMCA in July.
insights.speaker: mchalecki
insights.so_what: Precedent that USMCA status no longer guarantees exemption raises risk premia for cross-border auto, aerospace and defense supply chains.
insights.quote: Although the affected trade accounts for just about 5 percent of total imports, this sets an important precedent.

insights.claim: Canada is the largest buyer of US exports and US-Canada supply chains cross the border multiple times for autos, aircraft components and defense equipment, making a trade war especially costly.
insights.speaker: mchalecki
insights.so_what: Escalation hits integrated manufacturers on both sides; watch auto and aerospace suppliers.
insights.locator: Canada and the United States have many reasons

themes.theme: Rest of world keeps signing deals

insights.claim: Outside the US, FTAs remain in vogue: since January 2025 the EU has concluded deals with Mercosur (Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay, Uruguay) and India, India with New Zealand and the UK, and the UK with South Korea.
insights.speaker: mchalecki
insights.so_what: Trade diversion away from the US toward EU/India/UK networks — beneficiaries include exporters gaining preferential access to those blocs.
insights.quote: The United States is building economic walls.
